scope: Reward-only bounded overlay for current loaded DDR outputs; foci, layout and government systems are preserved.

foci.desc: Ulbricht's New Economic System promised enterprises greater responsibility for costs and results while the SED retained control of investment priorities. Better use of plant and machinery can raise output, but production targets still compete with consumer goods and the leadership's political timetable.

Honecker's social programme raises living standards through housing, wages, pensions and family support. It offers a popular alternative to investment-first planning, but recurring commitments narrow the funds available for industrial renewal and imports.

Gerhard Schürer's planners put real shortages, debt and investment bottlenecks before the party leadership. More credible accounting improves investment decisions, but ministries lose discretion and the report exposes failures the political centre would prefer to conceal.

foci.desc: The planners bind production targets to available materials, skilled labour and plant capacity. A more realistic plan improves factory performance, but additional reporting and central review carry an administrative cost.

Kombinate retain more responsibility for their own costs, export receipts and investment proposals. Enterprise managers gain room to improve output; without stronger worker oversight, the reform also expands their influence over public resources.

Guilds link independent craftspeople to local demand and preserve skills that state factories overlook. Their flexibility improves productivity, though a fragmented market makes trade with the central plan less predictable.

The Green League redirects investment away from the most polluting lignite plants and toward conservation and cleaner industrial practice. Health and agricultural conditions improve, but power shortages and resistance from the coal and chemical combines become harder to manage.

Christian social policy protects cooperative farms and small workshops as institutions rooted in local communities. A broader consumer economy can relieve shortages, but higher social commitments make rapid capital accumulation more difficult.

The social democrats promise secure employment, stronger services and a voice for organised labour. Their programme improves industrial productivity and household welfare, but expands the public obligations that future governments must finance.

The ESER programme coordinates computing standards and data processing with the socialist trading partners. A finite research grant supports electronics and computer engineering, while dependence on imported components remains a strategic weakness.

Schools and technical institutes introduce computer training to prepare a generation of engineers and production planners. The immediate benefit is a focused research opportunity; the long-term programme requires scarce equipment and qualified teachers.

A national conservation drive targets waste in homes, power plants and energy-intensive factories. Technical institutes and maintenance brigades coordinate retrofits, repairs and improvements to the energy network so that existing fuel supplies serve industry more efficiently.

Research into alternative power sources begins to reduce dependence on the lignite basin. A finite grant advances reactor engineering and raises the value of future investment; it builds no reactor, mine or uranium supply by itself.

Separating crop production from livestock specialisation allows larger LPGs to coordinate machinery, fodder and processing. Farm output improves, but the disruption to village routines strains cooperative members and their local representatives.

The NVA professionalises planning and unit readiness within the Warsaw Pact command structure. Shared manuals, staff exercises and standardised training strengthen unit organisation and provide a foundation for further doctrinal development.

Combined exercises with Soviet and Warsaw Pact formations teach officers to coordinate armour, artillery and infantry under pressure. The experience improves operational readiness and tactical learning, while the force remains committed to alliance plans.

foci.desc: Territorial defence prepares the NVA and local formations to hold key approaches while the main force mobilises. Dispersed readiness improves defence and mobilisation, while the existing focus cost and conscription trade-offs remain in force.

Soviet-pattern anti-tank and air-defence systems become common standards for NVA procurement and domestic production. Shared specifications simplify replacement stocks and local manufacture, while armoured-infantry research follows the same military tradition.

The 40th Parachute Battalion prepares for rapid deployment and operations behind the front. Specialist equipment and intensive training strengthen a small elite force, whose readiness places additional demands on the personnel budget.

Combat swimmers support Baltic reconnaissance, harbour security and specialised coastal operations. The force gains focused naval and special-forces training, but these small units cannot replace conventional fleet strength.

Patrols, observation posts and the NVA command system adopt common training and mobilisation procedures. More efficient personnel management improves frontier readiness, while the wider security apparatus requires a larger policing budget.

Coastal forces and air defence coordinate the Baltic approaches within Warsaw Pact planning. Common readiness procedures strengthen fleet organisation, protect ports and airfields, and connect the work of naval staffs with ground-based air defence.

The MiG-21 forms the backbone of a compact fighter force. Aircrew schools and technical institutes coordinate tactical flying, aircraft research and conversion training to make the most of the existing wings.

foci.desc: The MiG-23 gives the air force a more capable interceptor for contested airspace. New air-to-air weapons and defensive flying techniques strengthen its combat role, but demanding conversion training raises the risk of accidents.

The state concentrates investment on advanced production equipment and the industrial use of microelectronics. Key plants gain more reliable output, while scarce capital and consumer goods remain tied to a narrow set of priorities.

Industrial intensification pushes existing machinery closer to its technical limits. Better factory performance raises output from current capacity, but the effort depends on spare parts and disciplined maintenance.

The successors inherit the planning system with its export targets, investment obligations and hidden bottlenecks. A more productive industrial base and lower capital costs create room for recovery, but the Kombinate still compete for scarce imports.
Socialist thrift curbs waste and preserves resources for essential production. Household consumption becomes more affordable, but lower expectations and constrained trade weigh on public confidence.

Party leaders accept limits on their own privileges to defend the credibility of austerity. Cleaner administration and lower consumer pressure help the plan, while the SED apparatus resists losing its customary claims on state resources.
Defence industry receives first claim on investment and production targets. The NVA gains a stronger industrial base, while consumer production and civilian investment move further down the plan.

Stable retail prices become a political pledge to workers and their families. The state channels more of its resources into subsidies and social support to defend that pledge, easing immediate political pressure while increasing its fiscal obligations.

Native previews show the exact current-GDP treasury deduction, shared slots before all building levels, concrete old and new effects, limited research rewards, and project trade-offs while the focus is locked.

transactions.desc: The New Economic System directs capital toward bottleneck industries and export capacity. New chemical and civilian plant in Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt strengthens the investment-first course, while the price is paid from current national output and household consumption loses priority.

Kombinate receive greater authority to coordinate production, maintenance and investment across their plants. The larger industrial base improves civilian output, but enterprise managers gain influence over public resources and the party must police new accounting privileges.

The State Planning Commission equips the Dresden industrial region to process production data and coordinate technical targets. Computing research and office capacity improve planning, though skilled staff and equipment are diverted from other sectors.

Wage and pension commitments are backed by better transport links and housing access across Berlin, Brandenburg, Mecklenburg and Saxony-Anhalt. Household confidence rises, while the recurring social obligations narrow room for investment and increase demand on public services.

The housing drive expands the construction industry and the roads and utilities serving Berlin and the industrial regions. New works and better infrastructure support the supply of building materials, while the social commitments of the programme weigh on the state budget.

The leadership treats rising living standards as a central measure of socialist legitimacy. Housing infrastructure and civilian plant across Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Saxony support employment and supply, but the higher social commitment competes directly with industrial renewal and exports.

Everyday shortages expose the weaknesses of an economy organised around heavy industrial targets. Expanding civilian factories and improving their efficiency gives the plan a broader productive base, while committing scarce investment to the needs of households.

transactions.desc: The microelectronics resolution concentrates semiconductor and electronics research in Saxony. New plants and specialised institutes strengthen a strategic industrial sector, while the investment and the resources allocated to it compete with other civilian priorities.

Planning offices coordinate production data, supply targets and economic reporting from Berlin. Computing capacity and technical productivity improve, but offices absorb engineers and resources that could have expanded direct production.

The Schkopau chemical complex expands plastics and synthetic materials for machinery, construction and consumer goods. The refinery supports industrial independence, while feedstock dependence and pollution remain costly constraints.

Lusatian lignite supplies dispatchable electricity when imported fuels are scarce. The additional power station supports energy-intensive production, but pollution and public-health costs deepen dependence on the dirtiest domestic fuel.

Greifswald anchors a nuclear programme intended to reduce dependence on lignite. Reactor construction and specialist research expand generating capacity, but the investment must compete with other demands on the state budget and requires the necessary reactor technology.

The Green League invests in renewable generation and conservation instead of expanding lignite or nuclear power. Cleaner energy improves health and reduces waste, but the transition costs more and supplies less dependable power during the build-up.

Agricultural districts in Brandenburg coordinate machinery, storage and local food processing across cooperative farms. Rural output and local revenue improve, but the state commits scarce investment to the countryside and must balance local initiative with collective planning.

The Suhl arms industry receives new production capacity for the NVA and its Warsaw Pact obligations. Military output and tax receipts rise, but consumer production and civilian investment lose priority under a defence-first plan.

The CDU's Christian social-market programme expands civilian industry and household employment in Berlin. Local enterprise and social protection gain room to grow, but the state assumes larger obligations and must negotiate with established industrial combines.

The guild programme finances workshops and civilian industry in Thuringia and Saxony. Productive local enterprises broaden the revenue base and loosen the pressure of central allocation, while the state commits a substantial investment to their expansion.

The DBD strengthens roads and services in Mecklenburg's cooperative countryside. Better infrastructure supports agricultural production and village life, but construction competes with urban housing and industrial investment for public funds.
